scenes.tts: The first film showed oxygen changing what V H L could recognize. Why does one ubiquitin mark move a protein while another destroys it? Keep the same colors: yellow ubiquitin, grey targets, green E 3, and red proteasome.
scenes.caption: The first film showed oxygen changing what VHL could recognize. Why does one ubiquitin mark move a protein while another destroys it? Keep the same colors: yellow ubiquitin, grey targets, green E3 and red proteasome.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's color map exactly: ubiquitin yellow, targets grey, E3 green, signal gold, proteasome red. Begin with the final recognition diagram from the first film. Pull back to reveal three empty destination lanes around one grey target and place the opening question across the top.
scenes.narration: The first film showed oxygen changing what VHL could recognize. Why does one ubiquitin mark move a protein while another destroys it? Keep the same colors: yellow ubiquitin, grey targets, green E3 and red proteasome.

scenes.visual: Transform the three empty destination lanes into the title 'One Tag, Different Destinations' for two seconds. Shrink the title into the upper-left corner while one yellow ubiquitin continues orbiting the grey target.

scenes.tts: Start with one ubiquitin attached to one lysine. This monoubiquitin mark seldom sends a protein to the proteasome. It more often changes location. On a growth-factor receptor, readers can help pull the receptor into the cell by endocytosis.
scenes.caption: Start with one ubiquitin attached to one lysine. This monoubiquitin mark seldom sends a protein to the proteasome. It more often changes location. On a growth-factor receptor, readers can help pull the receptor into the cell by endocytosis.
scenes.visual: Transform the grey target into a large membrane receptor spanning a horizontal membrane. Attach one yellow ubiquitin below it. Reader blocks gather, the membrane bends smoothly around the receptor, and a vesicle pinches inward. Keep the red proteasome visible but inactive at far right.
scenes.narration: Start with one ubiquitin attached to one lysine. This monoubiquitin mark seldom sends a protein to the proteasome. It more often changes location. On a growth-factor receptor, readers can help pull the receptor into the cell by endocytosis.

scenes.tts: Now reconnect the yellow blocks into the classic proteasome-directed linkage. A sufficiently long chain is a usual proteasome signal. The red barrel engages the marked protein and breaks it down. This is the classic destruction route.
scenes.caption: Now reconnect the yellow blocks into the classic proteasome-directed linkage. A sufficiently long chain is a usual proteasome signal. The red barrel engages the marked protein and breaks it down. This is the classic destruction route.
scenes.visual: Reset the central target to a grey soluble block. Reconnect four yellow ubiquitin blocks into a chain labelled 'lysine 48'. Move the chain and target into the large red proteasome, then release small grey peptide blocks. Show the chain length on screen without speaking a numeral.
scenes.narration: Now reconnect the yellow blocks into the classic proteasome-directed linkage. A sufficiently long chain is a usual proteasome signal. The red barrel engages the marked protein and breaks it down. This is the classic destruction route.

scenes.tts: Reconnect the same yellow blocks through another linkage, and the picture changes again. Ubiquitin-binding domains clamp onto this chain. Several proteins can gather around one scaffold. Signaling complexes and repair proteins at damaged D N A can assemble this way.
scenes.caption: Reconnect the same yellow blocks through another linkage, and the picture changes again. Ubiquitin-binding domains clamp onto this chain. Several proteins can gather around one scaffold. Signaling complexes and repair proteins at damaged DNA can assemble this way.
scenes.visual: Pull the yellow blocks back from the proteasome and reconnect them into a differently angled chain labelled 'lysine 63'. Three large reader blocks with matching cup-shaped domains slide onto separate ubiquitins. The assembled complex fills most of the frame; label the example 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Reconnect the same yellow blocks through another linkage, and the picture changes again. Ubiquitin-binding domains clamp onto this chain. Several proteins can gather around one scaffold. Signaling complexes and repair proteins at damaged DNA can assemble this way.

scenes.tts: Return to a receptor carrying only one yellow ubiquitin. Is that single mark enough to commit the receptor to the proteasome? Choose a destination before the picture moves.
scenes.caption: Return to a receptor carrying only one yellow ubiquitin. Is that single mark enough to commit the receptor to the proteasome? Choose a destination before the picture moves.
scenes.visual: Center the monoubiquitinated receptor between a membrane-vesicle lane and the red proteasome lane. Draw equal dashed arrows toward both and place the question above. Keep both destinations neutral, with no highlight or motion toward either answer.
scenes.narration: Return to a receptor carrying only one yellow ubiquitin. Is that single mark enough to commit the receptor to the proteasome? Choose a destination before the picture moves.

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction frame for four and a half seconds. A thin countdown arc advances without numbers while the receptor gently bobs and both destination arrows remain neutral.

scenes.tts: Not usually. In this example, the single mark helps route the receptor into a vesicle. Movement and destruction can still cooperate later, because internalized receptors are often carried to lysosomes. The mark suggests an outcome; it does not guarantee one alone.
scenes.caption: Not usually. In this example, the single mark helps route the receptor into a vesicle. Movement and destruction can still cooperate later, because internalized receptors are often carried to lysosomes. The mark suggests an outcome; it does not guarantee one alone.
scenes.visual: Clear the proteasome arrow and animate the receptor into a vesicle. Then extend a dotted path from that vesicle toward a separate lysosome block, not the red proteasome. Add a small label 'typical here, not guaranteed' while the receptor keeps moving.
scenes.narration: Not usually. In this example, the single mark helps route the receptor into a vesicle. Movement and destruction can still cooperate later, because internalized receptors are often carried to lysosomes. The mark suggests an outcome; it does not guarantee one alone.

scenes.tts: So ubiquitin behaves as a context-dependent code. Linkage, chain length, branching, substrate, and available readers all matter. A simple lookup table would show too much certainty. Keep the mark, its reader, and the target together.
scenes.caption: So ubiquitin behaves as a context-dependent code. Linkage, chain length, branching, substrate and available readers all matter. A simple lookup table would show too much certainty. Keep the mark, its reader and the target together.
scenes.visual: Arrange the vesicle route, lysine-48 route and lysine-63 scaffold as three large lanes. Slide small context labels beside them: linkage, length, branching, target, readers. Avoid checkmarks or absolute labels; add 'typical outcomes' across all three lanes.
scenes.narration: So ubiquitin behaves as a context-dependent code. Linkage, chain length, branching, substrate and available readers all matter. A simple lookup table would show too much certainty. Keep the mark, its reader and the target together.

scenes.tts: A signal can also change recognition without modifying the target first. In plants, T I R 1 is a green E 3 receptor. An Aux I A A repressor rests nearby, but their contact is weak without the hormone auxin.
scenes.caption: A signal can also change recognition without modifying the target first. In plants, TIR1 is a green E3 receptor. An Aux/IAA repressor rests nearby, but their contact is weak without the hormone auxin.
scenes.visual: Transform the three routing lanes into one close-up interface. Build a large green TIR1 cup at left and a grey Aux/IAA repressor at right. Their surfaces leave a visible gap, so gentle ambient motion separates them. Keep yellow ubiquitin and red proteasome waiting in the background.
scenes.narration: A signal can also change recognition without modifying the target first. In plants, TIR1 is a green E3 receptor. An Aux/IAA repressor rests nearby, but their contact is weak without the hormone auxin.

scenes.tts: Auxin fits into a pocket exactly where T I R 1 and the repressor meet. The small gold signal fills their gap. Their grip tightens without building a separate cascade. Auxin acts as molecular glue at the target-receptor interface.
scenes.caption: Auxin fits into a pocket exactly where TIR1 and the repressor meet. The small gold signal fills their gap. Their grip tightens without building a separate cascade. Auxin acts as molecular glue at the target-receptor interface.
scenes.visual: Move one small gold auxin block into the gap. The green cup and grey repressor close around it as one continuous transformation. Enlarge the joint until it fills most of the frame and label the gold block 'auxin' and the complete contact 'molecular glue'.
scenes.narration: Auxin fits into a pocket exactly where TIR1 and the repressor meet. The small gold signal fills their gap. Their grip tightens without building a separate cascade. Auxin acts as molecular glue at the target-receptor interface.

scenes.tts: The ligase now ubiquitinates the repressor, and the proteasome removes it. Auxin-responsive genes are released from repression. Here hormone detection and target recruitment happen in one binding step. The signal triggers destruction by tightening an E 3 grip.
scenes.caption: The ligase now ubiquitinates the repressor, and the proteasome removes it. Auxin-responsive genes are released from repression. Here hormone detection and target recruitment happen in one binding step. The signal triggers destruction by tightening an E3 grip.
scenes.visual: Carry the closed TIR1-repressor pair back into the full pathway. Add a yellow ubiquitin chain to the grey repressor, then move only that repressor into the red proteasome. A large gene-control panel changes from repressed to active as the repressor disappears; mark the panel 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The ligase now ubiquitinates the repressor, and the proteasome removes it. Auxin-responsive genes are released from repression. Here hormone detection and target recruitment happen in one binding step. The signal triggers destruction by tightening an E3 grip.

scenes.tts: These two ideas work together. The E 3 chooses a recognized target, while the ubiquitin mark recruits particular readers. Ubiquitin marks route proteins; molecular glues change what an E 3 grips. Follow both questions to predict a target's fate.
scenes.caption: These two ideas work together. The E3 chooses a recognized target, while the ubiquitin mark recruits particular readers. Ubiquitin marks route proteins; molecular glues change what an E3 grips. Follow both questions to predict a target's fate.
scenes.visual: Split the frame into two connected questions: a green grip labelled 'Which target?' and three yellow mark shapes labelled 'Which readers?'. Flow both arrows into the three destination lanes. Land the film's own rule once, then fade everything except the color-matched symbols.
scenes.narration: These two ideas work together. The E3 chooses a recognized target, while the ubiquitin mark recruits particular readers. Ubiquitin marks route proteins; molecular glues change what an E3 grips. Follow both questions to predict a target's fate.

scenes.visual: End card on the dark ground with Hex beside one centered line only: 'Ubiquitin marks route proteins; molecular glues change what an E3 grips.'
